sentences.text: Fourteen thousand, nine hundred and seventy-five nights, and the ledger is one short.
I know who is missing.
I counted her out myself, when I was seven, and I let her drown.
I am Maren Voss, the tide clerk of Harrow Deep.
Tonight a storm tide broke into the strongroom, and the oldest ledger floated off its shelf, smelling of lamp oil.
I opened it to the night it happened, expecting one line in a child's hand.
I found two pages.
Twice a day, for about six hours each time, a stone road lies open to the mainland.
A bell on a post rings when the water turns.
Beside it hangs a short rope, for anyone the sea has caught.
My work is two columns.
A person who walks out is a stroke on the left, and that is OUT.
A person who walks home is a name on the right, and that is IN.
The columns must agree, and they have not agreed since I was seven.
The village calls the difference the Ghost.
They say the drowned clerk walks the road at night and rings for the one who is not home.
I do not believe in the Ghost.
I believe in arithmetic.
One went out.
One did not come back.
The first page was my mother's last night.
The second was dated for a night that had not happened yet.
The first page is plain.
The date is in my mother's hand, because she dated the week ahead every Sunday.
Below it is one stroke in the OUT column, in mine.
That stroke is her.
She crossed to the mainland at dusk for the morning medicine, because I had a fever.
At the door she turned and said, "Don't sleep, Maren. Count for me."
She smelled of wet wool and the peppermints she kept for the bell watch.
I counted her out, and I was proud of the stroke, because it was straight.
The IN column beside it has been empty for forty-one years.
The second page I never knew existed.
It carries the date of the following night.
In the right-hand column, in brown ink, in a hand that is mine at seven, all loops and pressure, there is an entry.
In one.
Beside it, where a name belongs, there is a space.
I do not remember writing it.
I remember the lamp, the fever, the rope in my fist.
After that, nothing.
I reasoned as a clerk reasons.
Somebody came home that night.
I wrote the figure and could not write the name.
A name I owe the book.
I allow no pencil in my book.
Yet every morning there is a grey smear on the new page, in the right column, and every morning I rub it out with a crust of bread.
Tonight I sat up with the ledger and the lamp.
I woke in my chair with the bell still dying in the dark.
My hem was stiff with salt.
The Ghost rings at the dead of low water, when the moon stands over the road.
I went to the window and looked at the road.
Nobody was on it.
The village has an answer for the bell.
Visitors see lamps on the causeway some nights, small and slow, in a row.
I do not accept lamps.
I accept evidence.
I keep an atlas of the causeway, because wet sand holds a print for hours, and a print is a fact.
In forty-one years it has recorded every boot, every dog, and one cart.
It has recorded no ghost.
Wenna, at the lamp shop, would not turn round from her wicks.
I took the second page to Kell, the ferryman.
His thumb was grey with graphite, from the pencil he keeps behind his ear for the nets.
He looked at the table.
He did not look at the page.
"Nobody came home that night, Maren," he said.
"That is why you keep the book."
So the bell rang, the road was empty, and the ledger was one short.
Three facts that cannot all be true.
I decided to remove the one fact I could control.
Myself.
At seven I fell asleep once, with the rope in my hand.
I would not sleep again.
I took a length of chain from the harbour store and set my desk where the line comes through the wall.
One end went round the desk leg.
The other went round my left ankle.
A chain is not for keeping something out.
It is for staying put when the body would rather go.
At the dead of low water the bell rings.
The lamps come out on the road.
The road is empty.
I turned the key and hung it on a cord round my neck.
I began to count.
The sea shushed against the stone like someone asking it to be quiet.
When the tide turned, I pulled the line, and the bell spoke across the black water.
Nobody was out there to hear it.
I wrote the word "nobody".
At the dead of low water, the lamps came.
Through the shutter I saw eleven small flames walking down from the village in no hurry.
They stopped at my door.
I heard breathing, and a woman say, "Not tonight."
Then the lamps turned and went back up the hill.
The bell did not ring.
I wrote two words.
Bell silent.
At dawn I turned the key.
My ankle was raw, a red band like a bracelet.
I did not remember pulling.
The new page had no grey smear.
In forty-one years it had never once been clean.
No prankster.
No walker.
The gap was not a nightly crime.
It was one old night, and I would have to go back and stand in it.
I opened the atlas to that dawn.
Two sets of prints came in from the sea.
A woman's boots, the left heel worn.
Beside them, small and bare, a child's.
In the margin the harbour keeper had written a line about the bell.
I skipped it as weather.
At the post, the small prints went on toward the village.
The large ones stopped.
Two heels, planted deep, facing the village lamps.
I did not close my eyes.
I went out to the Drowning Stone, because stone does not talk.
The Drowning Stone is ruled like a ledger.
I had never come close enough to see it.
It stands beyond the post, where the road dips, and at low water it shows its whole back, black and wet.
Up close it is cut with short strokes, packed edge to edge.
Forty-one rows, one for each year, and in each row a stroke for every night.
I walked to the end of the newest row.
Stroke after stroke after stroke, a thumb's width apart, one place for every night.
The last stroke was two nights old.
The place for last night was smooth.
I knew which night.
I walked back to the post.
I had pulled that line from the hut ten thousand times.
I had never stood where the short rope hangs and looked at it from the sea.
It was polished flat, as if a thumb had been drawn along it for decades.
On one side only.
The sea side.
A rope pulled from the hut wears all round.
This one had been pulled by someone standing out on the road with her back to the water, always with the same hand.
I laid my palm in the groove.
My fingers closed over the shine as though it had been cut for them.
I am left-handed.
For forty-one years I had listened for a ghost on the road.
The one who walks the causeway every night, and is never written down, is the clerk.
The OUT that was never counted was me.
The tide clock turned.
I did not hear the bell.
I wanted the feet.
That evening I scattered flour across the hut floor, from the bed to the door.
I did not chain my ankle.
I lay down in my clothes with my eyes open as long as I could keep them.
In the morning the flour had a path in it.
Bare feet, the second toe longer than the first.
From the bed to the door.
The door was latched from outside.
I followed the prints along the crown of the road on my knees.
Every fifth step they leaned a little to the left, as if someone were walking with a hand held out.
They reached the post and stopped, facing the village.
Then more prints.
Boots, a ring of them, around mine.
They had not trodden on one print of mine.
I sat on the wet stone and let it be true.
She walks barefoot every night, and the flood tide takes her prints before I wake.
The small bare prints in the atlas.
They were mine.
But a woman who finds her child on a closing road carries her home and shuts the door.
Her heels did not go home.
I could not make that sentence add up, so I put it aside.
I went back to the rope, because a rope remembers.
Under the bright groove of my own left hand there was another.
Older.
Deeper.
Higher up the rope, at the reach of a taller woman.
And worked into the strands, grey wool.
I knew only one coat that colour.
My mother's coat hangs on the peg behind my hut door, where it has hung since the tide brought it back, a week after.
I held the left cuff to the fibres from the rope.
The same grey.
The same twist.
The cuff was worn through, the way a sleeve wears when a hand has pulled hard on something wet.
Then I read the keeper's margin line.
He had written that the bell kept ringing after the road shut.
The line was slack at the hut.
A slack line means no hand at the hut.
In the strongroom I held a lamp low across the ledgers.
Ink sits on paper.
Pencil sinks into it.
In the IN column of every page there was a groove.
Kell's square strokes.
Wenna's round ones.
Hands I did not know.
That was the grey smear on my new page each dawn, rubbed out with bread for forty-one years.
That night I sat on the Stone with a dark lantern and watched my own hut.
At the dead of low water, the door opened.
A woman came out in a white nightdress, barefoot, her left hand held a little away from her side.
She walked like someone being led by the smell of home.
She went to the post, took the short rope in her left hand, and rang the bell.
It rang for a long time.
It sounded like what it was, a call to somebody still out in the dark.
Then the lamps came down the hill, eleven of them.
They made a ring around her, not touching.
Kell took her elbow so gently that she did not stir.
Wenna held a lamp to her face and said, "There you are."
Kell stayed.
He took the pencil from behind his ear.
He opened my book on the desk, found the new page, and wrote in the right column.
In one.
He wrote it the way a man writes his own name.
He looked up and saw me in the doorway.
He held out the pencil.
At the next low water I went to the post.
I stood on its sea side, my back to the water, and took the short rope in my left hand.
I rang the bell as the tide began to climb.
The sea came over the stone and found my ankles.
It was colder than I had allowed for.
It climbed my shins, and then my knees, and the rope grew heavy in my fist.
My palm lay in the worn groove.
Beside it, under my little finger, was the second groove, deeper, cut by a sleeve.
I looked toward the village lamps, the way a small child would have gone, barefoot, asleep, with the bell going behind her.
It is a long road for small legs.
The child was me.
Kell was waiting at the dry end, nineteen, running the wall with a lantern.
The bell rang until the water reached the clapper.
A drowned bell speaks once more.
He heard it speak.
I was across.
She was not.
The cold opened the door the years had locked.
She came back across in the last light, with medicine in her coat.
The hut was empty.
She followed small bare prints to the Stone and found me standing in the water.
She took my hand and walked me to the post, and turned me to face the lamps.
She took the short rope.
The sea was at her knees.
She rang, and I walked.
When I reached the dry stones she said it again, as she had at the door.
"Don't sleep, Maren. Count for me."
I counted my way home.
I wrote the figure on the next page, since a clerk does not write beneath the closing rule.
I left a space for the name and went to bed.
Kell wrote the figure in pencil on the first clean page, and Wenna on the next, one of them every night for forty-one years.
A child who learns she walks into the sea never sleeps again, so they chose the pencil over the telling, even on the chained night.
I had rubbed out every one.
I opened the old ledger to the second page.
In the blank, in a hand that did not shake, I wrote my own name.
Maren Voss.
Then I turned back to the straight stroke of a proud child in the OUT column and inked a name over it.
The first name that column has ever held.
Elin Voss.
At dusk a boy was late back from the cockle beds, and I rang the bell until he was across.
On the page for night fourteen thousand, nine hundred and seventy-nine, one went out and one came in, and the columns agreed.
On tomorrow's page I wrote in pencil, In one.
Just in case.
I was never the one who failed to count.
I was the one who was counted.
